analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to speed up and publicly report how they approve or deny seniors' care.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to speed up Medicare Advantage care approvals died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly all Medicare seniors are in private Medicare Advantage plans, which decide whether to approve care before doctors can provide it — and those plans decide how long patients wait. This bill would have required those plans to use a standardized electronic system for approval requests, respond within timeframes set by the Health Secretary, and publicly report each year, plan by plan, how many requests they approve or deny, how long they take, how often denials are overturned on appeal, and when they use artificial intelligence to make decisions. Patients would also gain the right to see the criteria a plan uses to deny their care.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors in Medicare Advantage plans who wait on approval decisions for care, and the doctors and suppliers who navigate those requests. More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage plans, so delays and denials affect a very large group of older Americans; the bill would also benefit them indirectly by giving regulators and the public plan-by-plan data on denials and on the use of AI in those decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans would have to run prior authorization requests through a standardized electronic system with defined response timeframes, rather than fax and portal delays.

Plans must report annually, on a public website, how often they approve or deny requests for each item and service, how long decisions take, how often denials are overturned on appeal, and when they use artificial intelligence or automated decision-making — making denial practices visible for the first time.

Enrollees gain the right to see the criteria a plan uses to decide their requests, and plans must review their prior authorization lists every year with input from patients and providers, with the possibility of waiving requirements for well-performing providers.
The Secretary could set binding timeframes — such as 24 hours — for plan decisions, including expedited and routine requests.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who would bear the cost of building electronic approval systems and publishing their denial and appeal data — costs they might partly pass to premiums. Doctor's offices would face an adjustment to new electronic workflows, though many providers supported the bill because it would cut their fax-and-portal paperwork.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban or limit any prior authorization requirement — plans could keep denying care as long as they disclose it electronically and on time, so it regulates rather than restricts the practice.

Compliance costs fall on Medicare Advantage insurers and the doctors' offices that must adopt new electronic systems, and insurers argue some of those costs are ultimately passed back into premiums or plan benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is administrative: MA plans must build electronic prior authorization systems and report extensive data, and some of that cost may be passed on. Some providers also worry that standardizing prior authorization could implicitly endorse its use rather than shrink it. But the patient benefit — faster decisions, visible denial data, curbs on opaque AI-driven denials — is substantial and overdue for the tens of millions of beneficiaries in MA. On balance the benefits clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the congressional session ended — no committee vote, no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 13, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee — the only action it ever received.
It carried 59 Senate cosponsors from both parties, including 32 Democrats, 26 Republicans, and 1 Independent.
The Finance Committee never took it up, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: the bill that would have required them to disclose and speed up their care denials died in committee without a vote.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on June 13, 2024.

for.name: 59 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Senators from both parties (32 D, 26 R, 1 I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it enough support to pass the Senate if it had reached the floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it remained referred to the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The 59 cosponsors split 32 Democrats, 26 Republicans, and 1 Independent — unusually broad, bipartisan support for a bill that never got a vote.

industries.note: The bill forces these insurers to build electronic prior authorization systems, disclose their denial and appeal rates publicly, and accept federal decision timeframes — reducing a key tool for holding down spending by delaying or denying care. Seniors gain timely access at the insurers' administrative expense.
Doctors and suppliers currently spend staff time chasing approvals by fax and proprietary portals; standardized electronic prior authorization and published criteria would cut that paperwork burden.
A mandate for standardized electronic prior authorization creates a compliance market for health information technology vendors building the transmission systems.
